rows.standfirst: How did the U.S. become the Olympic powerhouse it is today? Cold War competition. The Soviet Union sponsored their athletes. But America wanted its athletes to pull themselves up by their bootstraps. It birthed an unexpected accelerator of Olympic development: College football. Stay with us now.

rows.title: Researchers say no evidence of TikTok censorship, but they remain wary

rows.title: Bezos orders deep job cuts at 'Washington Post'

rows.title: You owe it to yourself to go on a solo trip. Here's how to plan one
rows.standfirst: Traveling on your own can be scary, but it can be one of the most meaningful things you can do for yourself. Three solo travelers share their experiences — and what makes for a successful trip.

rows.title: Warming your house the green way just got more expensive

rows.title: U.S. unexpectedly adds 130,000 jobs in January after a weak 2025
rows.standfirst: U.S. employers added 130,000 jobs in January as the unemployment rate dipped to 4.3% from 4.4% in December. Annual revisions show that job growth last year was far weaker than initially reported.

rows.title: What is going on with gold and silver?
rows.standfirst: The prices of gold and silver are on rollercoaster rides; Gold has been rising over the last few years, silver shot up like a skyrocket in January … but then both plunged in price and sputtered around the end of the month.

rows.title: How much power does the Fed chair really have?
rows.standfirst: On paper, the Fed chair is just one vote among many. In practice, the job carries far more influence. We analyze what gives the Fed chair power.

rows.title: The boxed meal helping Americans stay on budget
rows.standfirst: Food keeps getting more expensive, so how do shoppers respond? They change what they buy, right? It’s not just that cheaper foods get more popular. Shoppers are more nuanced than that. So, today on the show, we choose one classic meal that is tailor-made for this anxious economic moment. Why Hamburger Helper is poised to win 2026.

rows.title: A shadowy industry is helping small businesses pay tariffs — at a high cost
rows.standfirst: How about $350,000 within hours? The pitches flood small businesses: "No hidden fees, No BS." These financial lifelines are barely regulated and can turn into trip wires.

rows.title: Are we in an economic 'doom loop'?
rows.standfirst: Trade wars. Financial panics. Inflation. How come it feels like it’s all bad news in the global economy these days? Economist Eswar Prasad’s answer: something he calls the ‘doom loop.’ That’s where massive geopolitical and economic forces feed off each other and send us careening into disorder. Sounds dire. But it’s not hopeless.

rows.title: FCC calls for more 'patriotic, pro-America' programming in run-up to 250th anniversary
rows.standfirst: The "Pledge America Campaign" urges broadcasters to focus on programming that highlights "the historic accomplishments of this great nation from our founding through the Trump Administration today."

rows.title: Trump excoriates Supreme Court justices after tariff loss
rows.standfirst: The battle over the tariffs began on day one of the president's second term when he signed an executive order that let him impose a wide range of tariffs on virtually every U.S. trading partner.

rows.title: Can I get my tariff money back now?
rows.standfirst: The Supreme Court struck down a bunch of President Trump’s tariffs yesterday. The Trump administration originally used an emergency economic powers law to justify the tariffs. And the court said: No! You can’t do that! Bad Trump, bad! This is despite the U.S. having raked in over a hundred billion dollars in import taxes already.

rows.title: After the Supreme Court's ruling on tariffs, companies line up for refunds
rows.standfirst: The Supreme Court on Friday struck down President Trump's tariffs. But the justices left a $133 billion question unanswered: What's going to happen to the money the government has already collected?

rows.title: The economy slowed in the last 3 months of the year — but was still solid in 2025
rows.standfirst: The U.S. economy grew 2.2% in 2025, a modest slowdown from 2.4% the previous year. GDP gains were fueled by solid consumer spending and business investment.

rows.title: Using saliva to detect disease holds promise, but it's not perfected yet
rows.standfirst: Easier than a blood test, saliva tests have the potential to detect cavities, infections and even cancer. But a lack of insurance coverage and other obstacles stand in the way of wider use.

rows.title: Amazon dethrones Walmart as the world's biggest company by sales
rows.standfirst: In a slow-motion race of two retail behemoths, Amazon's trump card was its lucrative cloud-computing business.

rows.title: U.K.'s ex-Prince Andrew is released after his arrest over Epstein revelations
rows.standfirst: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the British former prince, was released after spending the day in police custody but is still under investigation on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

rows.title: How do Olympians like Eileen Gu earn $23 million? Here are all the ways
rows.standfirst: Most Olympians never win big money — or big fame. So how are athletes such as Eileen Gu or Chloe Kim able to earn millions of dollars? Here are some of the ways.

rows.title: Why this rural town wants an ICE facility
rows.standfirst: The Trump administration is planning to pour more than $38 billion into warehouses for mass immigrant detention. While some communities are starting to push back, one rural town has agreed to expand its detention facility. On today’s show, we visit a small town in Georgia to learn about the trade-offs of becoming a detention town.

rows.title: Zuckerberg grilled about Meta's strategy to target 'teens' and 'tweens'
rows.standfirst: The billionaire tech mogul's testimony was part of a landmark social media addiction trial in Los Angeles. The jury's verdict in the case could shape how some 1,600 other pending cases from families and school districts are resolved.

rows.title: How could the U.S. war in Iran affect the world's oil supply?
rows.standfirst: Despite sanctions, Iran is one of the world's major oil producers, with much of its crude exported to China.

rows.title: Don't hate the replicator, hate the game
rows.standfirst: The world of science has been stuck in an existential crisis over whether we actually know the things we thought we knew. Re-running an old study today doesn't always yield the same result. Same with re-enacting old experiments. Collectively, this is known as the “replication crisis.”

rows.title: OpenAI announces Pentagon deal after Trump bans Anthropic
rows.standfirst: Shortly after the president's ban of artificial intelligence company Anthropic, rival OpenAI announced it had done a deal with the Defense Department to provide its technology for classified networks.

rows.title: Paramount and Warner Bros' deal is about merging studios, and a whole lot more

rows.title: These major issues have brought together Democrats and Republicans in states

rows.title: Mortgage rates fall below 6% for the first time in years

rows.title: Why farmers in California are backing a giant solar farm
rows.standfirst: Many farmers have had to fallow land as a state law comes into effect limiting their access to water. There's now a push to develop some of that land … into solar farms.

rows.title: Trump's tariffs likely cost you hundreds of dollars. Will you get a refund?

rows.title: Every business wants your review. What's with the feedback frenzy?
rows.standfirst: Customers want to read reviews and businesses need reviews to attract customers. But the constant demand for reviews could be creating a feedback backlash, experts say.

rows.title: How your favorite fish sticks might be funding Russia's war
